title: Judges: a people coming apart

lines: Judges covers the years after Joshua and before the kings.
A generation grows up not knowing the LORD. And the book becomes an honest account of a people coming apart, and of a God who wouldn't give them up.

scripture.text: another generation rose up who did not know the LORD or the works that He had done for Israel.

lines: An opening shows the land half taken and sets out a pattern. Then come the judges: from Othniel to Gideon, from Abimelech to Jephthah, and Samson.
The last five chapters have no judge at all. The beginning and the end answer each other.

scripture.text: Then the LORD raised up judges

lines: Chapter two sets out a wheel. Israel serves other gods. Raiders come. The people cry out. And God raises up a judge. Then it starts again.
Mercy holds the wheel up, but it runs downhill. It's a spiral, not a circle.

scripture.text: for the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning

lines: Look who God uses. A left-handed man. A woman. A farmer threshing in a winepress. The son of a prostitute. And a man who breaks nearly every vow.
The deliverance is God's, carried out through very human hands.

chapters.kicker: Watch for: gifts are not goodness
lines: The Spirit of the LORD comes on Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson. But power isn't character. Gideon makes an object all Israel worships. Jephthah's rash vow costs his daughter.
Judges never treats God's gift as approval.

scripture.text: it became a snare to Gideon and his household.

chapters.kicker: Watch for: no king in Israel
lines: The last chapters tell of a stolen idol, an outrage at Gibeah, and a civil war. The book presents them as the depths, never as a pattern.
In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

scripture.text: In those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

lines: Readers weigh several of these stories in more than one way, and they differ on what that last line is asking for: a king, the LORD's own rule, or both.
On every reading, the book gives no nation, no church, and no person a warrant for violence against anyone.
Start with chapter two, slowly. Then the key chapters: four, six, nine, eleven, sixteen, and twenty-one.
Watch the refrains. Don't take the judges as models. And don't read the hard chapters alone.
Judges doesn't end with a solution. It ends with a need.
